HEADLINE: ACT and WA winners, SA, Tas the losers
INTRO: States with higher income earners such as the ACT and Western Australia could be the winners in a fundamental overhaul of income tax collection, while people living in South Australia and Tasmania would be the losers.
TEXT:
States with higher income earners such as the ACT and Western Australia could be the winners in a fundamental overhaul of income tax collection, while people living in South Australia and Tasmania would be the losers.

Neil Warren, a leading expert on state-federal financial relations, has previously modelled scenarios in which state and territory governments were able to levy extra income tax from residents to raise $10 billion, or $445 per taxpayer.

The University of NSW tax professor found that for Tasmania to raise $445 per person in 2011-12, the state government would have needed to impose a 10 per cent surcharge and South Australia an 8.9 per cent surcharge. NSW, Victoria and Queensland were between 6.8 and 7.8 per cent.

But WA, with is comparatively well-off population, would only have to impose a 5.3 per cent surcharge and the ACT 4.9 per cent.

"Perhaps not surprisingly, WA and the ACT would find it easier to implement a surcharge than Tasmania or South Australia," Professor Warren said.

The federal government has not yet outlined the specifics of its plan. But Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull is keen to discuss an income tax sharing model that would eventually allow states to adopt their own tax rates.

Professor Warren said such a proposal was challenging but possible.

"The key consideration is to be mindful of the circumstances of states such as South Australia and Tasmania whose situation is not of their making and who will always need some form of special assistance."

Changes to the way the Commonwealth Grants Commission operates would also be required, he said.

The commission, established in 1933, is responsible for recommending to the federal government each state's share of GST.

The idea is to redistribute revenue so Australians have potential access to the same level of service whether they live in Burnie, Brisbane or Bourke.

This is known as horizontal fiscal equalisation. Allowing states to collect and keep more tax, and therefore fund better services, would disrupt this fundamental premise.

The challenges were not insurmountable but would require "balancing harmony within the federation with creating the needed incentives for change", Professor Warren said.

"We have to have it such that if the states take risks, they get rewards," he said. "That doesn't really happen at the moment because if they take risks they have to share much of the rewards with other states and the Commonwealth."

A research paper published late in 2015 by Professor Warren and University of Tasmania political scientist Richard Eccelston cautioned that the flip side of interstate competition over income tax rates was the incentive for high-income earners to arrange their affairs so their state of residency for tax purposes differed from their actual place of residence.

To overcome this problem, some states in the United States defined income tax residency based on "more complex legal definitions of domicile informed by residency, ownership of real property, and sources of income", the paper noted.

HEADLINE: Time for arguing to stop, let's get delivering
INTRO: What Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull said on Wednesday about the government's tax plans:
TEXT:
What Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull said on Wednesday about the government's tax plans:

Australia's governments must work together to solve the big issues.

Our economic plan is designed to ensure that as our economy transitions from the mining boom to a wider and more diverse economy, we continue to deliver the vital services and infrastructure Australians expect.

In Canberra on Friday, I will meet with premiers and Territory chief ministers to discuss our plan to fund services in the years ahead, in the most effective way for all Australians. For you.

Currently, Canberra collects taxes and provides the states and territories almost $50 billion in tied grants each year to fund services and build infrastructure. This results in ongoing arguments, negotiations and duplication in administration.

In many areas, responsibility is far from clear and the only thing in ample supply is finger pointing and blame.We're all sick of it.

A way to solve this problem would be to give the states and territories a proportion of personal income tax - rather than demanding money from Canberra they would be raising money themselves and be accountable to their own voters. The focus of governments should be about delivering better services - not arguing over funding.

The key principle will be that this is not about increasing the total tax take - any income tax surrendered by the Commonwealth to the states would be offset by a reduction in Commonwealth grants to the states.

Taxpayers would not notice any administrative change - the Australian Tax Office would continue to manage the collection of income tax.

So, clearer lines of responsibility, less duplication, more open accountability.

The states' lack of financial freedom, their constant begging to the Commonwealth, the constant blame game - this is what is wrong with our federation. Now we can't reform it ourselves - this has to be agreed with the states and we know it will take time.

But the question for us all is this: do we want to keep complaining about the issue as we have done for decades, or do we want to do something about it?

Let's stop the predictable arguments, and focus instead on the best way to deliver effective services for all Australians.

HEADLINE: Wesfarmers probes Target deals
INTRO: Wesfarmers is investigating deals done with 30 foreign suppliers to discount department store Target that boosted profit by about 25 per cent in the first half on the condition that the money flow back to the suppliers through higher prices before the end of the financial year.
TEXT:
Wesfarmers is investigating deals done with 30 foreign suppliers to discount department store Target that boosted profit by about 25 per cent in the first half on the condition that the money flow back to the suppliers through higher prices before the end of the financial year.

Without them earnings would have slumped about 15 per cent instead of rising 5.7 per cent.

The supplier rebates were uncovered in the past few weeks by Guy Russo, who was given responsibility for both Kmart and Target as part of a restructure aimed at boosting the performance of Target.

Wesfarmers chief financial officer Terry Bowen said that payment of cash rebates from suppliers just prior to the end of a balance date was not the way Wesfarmers operates.

“We pride ourselves on the way we do business with suppliers,” he said.

HEADLINE: States resist Turnbull offer to tax incomes
SUBHEAD: Powers last used in 1942 - Would be used to fund health and education - PM promises long debate
INTRO: Key states have rejected a proposal by Malcolm Turnbull to let them individually levy their own income tax to fund health and education, but the Prime Minister said it was the only way to end the age-old funding squabbles with the states.
TEXT:
Key states have rejected a proposal by Malcolm Turnbull to let them individually levy their own income tax to fund health and education, but the Prime Minister said it was the only way to end the age-old funding squabbles with the states.

The proposal, to be put to a meeting on Friday of federal and state leaders and treasurers, would give the states taxing powers last used in 1942 and last proposed in 1991 by Bob Hawke.

It is designed to make the states fully responsible for funding schools and to force them to take a greater role in hospital funding.

The change could lead to as many as eight different personal income tax rates across the country, prompting concerns from business about increased complexity and reduced competitiveness due to income tax rate increases.

The Labor opposition said it made a mockery of a commitment to lower, simpler and fairer taxes and red tape reduction.

The plan was taken from the Abbott government’s Commission of Audit, which said the states needed to have greater autonomy over the services they administer but was dismissed at the time by prime minister Tony Abbott as double taxation.

The federal government would reduce income tax rates by about 2 percentage points. Each state and territory would then levy that amount back as an income tax surcharge to keep the income tax rates and the overall revenue intake unchanged.

Critically, Mr Turnbull said over time, each state could then increase the rate of its income tax surcharge, possibly under a cap, if it needed more revenue. Conversely, it could reduce it to gain a competitive edge over other states. There would also be extra pressure to be more efficient.

‘‘In future, in the longer term, a state should be free to lower that amount or indeed raise it and then they are accountable to their own voters," he said.

‘‘If we need more money, then they go, the state would go to their parliament, raise the money, go to the people and persuade them of the merits of it. This is a real opportunity to make the federation work. It will reduce an enormous amount of duplication and it will promote greater efficiency," he said.

‘‘Rather than demanding money from Canberra they would be raising money themselves and be accountable to their own voters.

"This, we believe, is the only way that we can genuinely reform our federation".

The announcement exposed further the tensions between Mr Turnbull and Treasurer Scott Morrison.

Mr Morrison, who helped develop the plan, said on Wednesday it was "key" that there be no overall increase in the tax burden. When told about Mr Turnbull’s comments regarding the states being able to lift their surcharge and, hence, the overall burden, he claimed the Prime Minister had "not gone that far, ultimately".

On Friday, the states will be offered more than $3 billion extra for health funding for the next four years to help redress the impact of the $80 billion in hospital and school funding cuts inflicted in the 2014 federal budget. But there will be no more money for schools and a source said the states could adopt the tax plan before 2020 if they wanted to increase school funding.

The proposal differs to an idea by South Australian Premier Jay Weatherill and NSW Premier Mike Baird for the states to receive a fixed share of income tax - which grows at a faster rate than the GST - and for the federal government to retain sole responsibility for the tax rate.

Mr Weatherill, Mr Baird and Tasmania’s Will Hodgman rejected the Turnbull idea while Western Australia’s Colin Barnett embraced it.

Victoria’s Daniel Andrews and Queensland’s Annastacia Palaszczuk were more open minded. Both have advocated increasing income taxes in the form of an increased Medicare surcharge as an alternative to raising the GST.

Mr Weatherill called the proposal "back to the future".

"I proposed the states get a fixed share of income tax but I think the idea of the states having their own income taxing powers again would create some form of double taxation. It’s just not practical, I don’t think it would work and I doubt whether the Commonwealth would seriously advance the proposal," he said.

Mr Baird said the federal proposal could be considered over the longer term.

"While I have historically argued for a share of income tax for the states, this has not involved increasing the income tax burden on Australian households, which already have among the highest income tax rates in the world," he said.

"These matters can be considered in the longer term. What is required right now is a partnership between the Commonwealth and the states for the health and education services we need."

Mr Hodgman said Tasmania would be disadvantaged.

‘‘If there’s any suggestion that the federal government will lower income tax and states like Tasmania will be expected to increase it, clearly that’s not workable and not something we would support,’’ he said.

‘‘We have been through this argument before with the GST. Tasmania is a small state, we will not be able to compete. We don’t want to get caught in a race to the bottom with larger states who are more able to raise their own taxation base and will use it in a way to game the system.’’

A spokesman for the Business Council of Australia said "we would be concerned about anything which risks increasing complexity reduces the competitiveness of Australia’s income tax system."

Shadow treasurer Chris Bowen said the government had become desperate. ‘‘Malcolm Turnbull and Scott Morrison promised lower, simpler, fairer taxes but proposals for state income taxes fulfil none of this criteria, and in fact will do the opposite, leading to higher and more complex taxes,’’ he said. ‘‘Mr Morrison made bracket creep his great moral challenge and yet the tax reform answer he’s now giving life to is for state governments to increase income taxes.

The states will not be asked to sign off on the tax proposal on Friday. Mr Turnbull said a debate would ensue. ‘‘This is a beginning of a journey. What we are talking about is the most fundamental reform to the Federation in generations," he said.

The states' lack of financial freedom, their constant begging to the Commonwealth, the constant blame game – this is what is wrong with our federation. PM Malcolm Turnbull

This is not a government that has any interest in lifting the tax burden on Australians. Treasurer Scott Morrison

As far as Victoria is concerned, Friday will not be about tax policy thought bubbles. Daniel Andrews, Vic

I think it's a good reform, not only for the states, it's a good reform for Australia. Colin Barnett, WA

This is Malcolm Turnbull's tax plan – a blank page. Annastacia Palaszczuk, Qld

If there's any suggestion that the government will lower income tax and states will be expected to increase it, clearly that's not workable and not something we would support. Will Hodgman, Tas

[It] would create some form of double taxation. It's just not practical, I don't think it would work and I doubt whether the Commonwealth would seriously advance the proposal. Jay Weatherill, SA

While I have historically argued for a share of income tax for the states, this has not involved increasing the income tax burden on households, which have among the highest rates in the world. Mike Baird, NSW

HEADLINE: The detail
INTRO: Senior sources say the Prime Minister is looking for an in-principle agreement with the premiers on Friday even if he has very clear ideas of where things should land.
TEXT:
Senior sources say the Prime Minister is looking for an in-principle agreement with the premiers on Friday even if he has very clear ideas of where things should land.

The idea is that the discussion would encapsulate health and schools funding, income-tax sharing and what the states should do about their own taxes.

Two sources said that schools funding was the obvious place where the federal government was likely to withdraw its involvement. This is because, the argument goes, it is a much cleaner area to break from than health, where there is complex overlap between hospital, primary care and aged-care funding.

Health funding changes could be pulled into the process, including a plan by Health Minister Sussan Ley on chronic care funding.

HEADLINE: Virgin-Air NZ divorce could trigger bid
INTRO: Air New Zealand’s chief executive has resigned from the board of Virgin Australia and put its 26 per cent stake up for sale, a decision that could trigger a takeover bid for Australia’s second-largest airline.
TEXT:
Air New Zealand’s chief executive has resigned from the board of Virgin Australia and put its 26 per cent stake up for sale, a decision that could trigger a takeover bid for Australia’s second-largest airline.

There has been growing concern about Virgin’s financial position since it tapped shareholders for a loan last week to further reduce gearing which appears to have been crystallised by the New Zealanders’ loss of confidence in the company.

In an extraordinary move, Air New Zealand appointed bankers to review its $350 million stake, including a possible sale. Air New Zealand chief Christopher Luxon resigned from the Virgin board effective immediately.

Air New Zealand is the biggest of Virgin’s four major shareholders, including three airlines, on Virgin’s tightly held share register. It has a 25.9 per cent stake, followed by Middle Eastern carrier Etihad with 25.1 per cent and Singapore Airlines with 22.2 per cent. Richard Branson’s Virgin Group owns about 10 per cent.

Air New Zealand, which is under competitive pressure from Qantas Airways and American Airlines, said it wanted to free up capital to fund growth.

Mr Luxon said in a statement he supported Virgin’s transformation, but he has privately expressed frustration with Virgin’s financial position and had been agitating for chief executive John Borghetti to step down.

‘‘A lot of us in the industry were wondering who would blink first,’’ Oliver Lamb, managing director at Ailevon Pacific Aviation Consulting, said, referring to the three airline shareholders.

‘‘Air New Zealand is in a situation for the first time in a long time where its strength in the New Zealand market has been put under a lot of pressure. It is looking at them and saying they could do better things with the capital themselves than having it tied up with Virgin.’’

Mr Borghetti still has the support of the Virgin board, sources said. An Etihad spokesman said on Wednesday the Abu Dhabi-based carrier fully supported Virgin’s strategy and management team. Etihad chief James Hogan appeared at a function with Virgin chairman Elizabeth Bryan on Wednesday night.

Mr Borghetti, a former Qantas senior executive, has spent five years turning the former budget airline into a premium carrier and growing in business travel. The airline returned to a profit in the first half of the current year and is expected to post a full-year profit around $115 million.

But analysts said there was concern money being raised was being used to reduce gearing rather than fund expansion.

Virgin last week obtained a 12-month $425 million unsecured loan from its four major shareholders, including Air New Zealand, to buy itself more time to fix its balance sheet as part of a broader review of its capital structure. Even if it sells its stake, Air New Zealand will be committed to the loan.

Virgin took out a $US125 million ($164 million) loan in the first half of the financial year amid a decline in its unrestricted cash balance to $544 million, from $839 million a year earlier.

Air New Zealand is expected to make a loss on its investment in Virgin. It owns 914 million shares, worth $310 million based on Virgin’s closing share price on Wednesday. Virgin’s stock fell 3.5¢ to 34¢ on Wednesday.

Deutsche Bank analysts said Air New Zealand acquired the stake for $NZ480 million, of which $NZ70 million had already been written off. Unless it sold its stake at a premium, it faced another $NZ60 million or more in losses.

‘‘While Virgin has made progress in recent times, there have been no dividends paid to Air New Zealand and there is a chance Virgin will require more capital in the future. Air New Zealand can use the capital in its own operations, or to de-gear the balance sheet,’’ Deutsche Bank analyst Matt Peek said.

The matter came to a head this week when Mr Luxon took his concerns to the board, which continues to support Mr Borghetti.

The move is expected to trigger a shake-up in the airline’s shareholder base, and possibly the biggest change to the Australian aviation market since Ansett’s collapse in 2001.

Air New Zealand could sell its stake to either Etihad or Singapore Airlines if minority shareholders supported the move. It could also mount a full takeover of the airline or sell the stake to a third partly, possibly a Chinese or American airline seeking to expand in the region.

‘‘All of a sudden there are a lot of cashed-up airlines out there in the world and the Australian market is still an attractive cornerstone asset,’’ Mr Lamb said.

Virgin America in the US is the subject of a takeover offer. Richard Branson’s Virgin Group is not expected to increase its stake in the Australian carrier.

HEADLINE: EY braces for work disruption
INTRO: EY is on track to grow more than 10 per cent this financial year, according to global chief executive and chairman, Mark Weinberger.
TEXT:
EY is on track to grow more than 10 per cent this financial year, according to global chief executive and chairman, Mark Weinberger.

The global professional services firm, which is holding its global partner meeting in Sydney this week, is bracing for a major upset in its workforce and marketplace over the next decade.

"Whatever you're studying today will probably be obsolete by the time you get out into the real world," Mr Weinberger said in an interview.

"The average age of an S&P500 company in the United States is 15 years," he said, alluding to the fact that many clients that EY services today either won't exist 20 years from now, or will be very different. "Kids are too caught up and worried about memorising everything on a test. That's not life." He believes learning how to learn, refining what you're good at, and honing collaborative abilities is a better way for workers to future-proof their careers.

EY is one of the world's largest professional services firms, with 220,000 staff in over 150 countries, and revenue of $US28.7 billion ($37.4 billion). It hires 60,000 people a year - one every 11 minutes - and the median age of its workforce is 29.

"If I as a leader don't recognise that they [employees] think differently, that the workplace of the future is going to be different, and that they need more flexibility - I can't have the most inspired workers. And workers are our only asset," Mr Weinberger said.

"The days of the imperial CEO are over. It's all about the team you create which has to be reflective of your employees and your marketplace."

EY wants 30 per cent of its revenue to come from emerging markets by 2020. It appointed a young female partner from Brazil to its global board last year, with the express aim of getting more thought diversity into its board to hit this goal. Age was a key factor in the appointment, according to Mr Weinberger.

Mr Weinberger's own path to CEO is an unusual one for a big four accounting firm, which typically anoint "lifers" to the top job. He worked in the US Senate, started his own lobbying and regulatory business, and served as President George W. Bush's assistant secretary of the Treasury for tax policy. In the process he left EY on three separate occasions.

Mr Weinberger believes the US will get on board with country-by-country reporting, and the faster the better.

However, he predicts an explosion in country-to-country disputes over tax dollars as a result of the OECD base erosion and profit shifting project.

He said the nub of the problem is that for a country to collect more tax, another has to take a haircut, and everyone expects to be a winner.

The other sticking point is the lack of a dispute resolution mechanism.

"The OECD project could not agree on an arbitration clause that would allow for dispute resolution of two countries. That's a really important ingredient of BEPS," Mr Weinberger said. "Without an arbitration clause you're setting up disputes between countries that corporations are going to be stuck right in the middle of."

HEADLINE: Probe into Target's supplier rebates
INTRO: Wesfarmers is investigating deals done with 30 foreign suppliers to discount department store Target, which boosted profit by about 25 per cent in the first half with the express condition that the money flow back to the suppliers through higher prices before the end of the financial year.
TEXT:
Wesfarmers is investigating deals done with 30 foreign suppliers to discount department store Target, which boosted profit by about 25 per cent in the first half with the express condition that the money flow back to the suppliers through higher prices before the end of the financial year.

The supplier rebate arrangements lifted Target's profit for the six months to December by between $US10 million and $US12 million ($13 million to $15 million).

Without the deals, the Target earnings before interest and tax for the first half would have slumped about 15 per cent instead of rising 5.7 per cent. The reported results were the best half-yearly profit performance at Target for three years. They were presented to the market as proof that the three-year transformation program under Target chief executive Stuart Machin was progressing well.

Machin was replaced in late February by former Kmart chief executive Guy Russo, who was given responsibility for both Kmart and Target as part of a restructure aimed at boosting Target's performance.

The supplier rebates were uncovered by Russo in the past few weeks during his initial examination of the business.

When the rebates were brought to the attention of Wesfarmers chief financial officer Terry Bowen, he ordered an investigation that is being led by Target's new chief financial officer Mark Scatena.

Normally, rebates paid by suppliers to Target are included in inventory for accounting purposes. They are not put through the profit and loss statement.

But in this case, the foreign suppliers who were approached to pay cash rebates to Target had supplied stock that had already been marked down and sold. The suppliers were asked to make the cash payments as part of a deliberate strategy to boost the company's profit margin and make the results for the half year look good.

The key twist in the deal was that letters were exchanged guaranteeing the money paid in rebates would be recovered in the second half of the financial year through higher prices. This sort of profit margin management has been common practice in the retail industry in Australia over the past five years. It was used by Woolworths in 2014 and referred to as "margin filling" by Woolworths staff.

Bowen told Chanticleer the payment of cash rebates from suppliers just prior to the balance date was "not the way we do business. We pride ourselves on the way we do business with suppliers," he said.

Machin was unavailable to comment on Wednesday as he was on a plane headed to Thailand for a holiday. However, earlier this month, he was keen to defend his track record at Target. But his promise to remain at Target until July was abandoned about a week after Russo took over.

Machin, who left Target on March 11, has been working in the Wesfarmers head office in Melbourne.

Bowen said that Wesfarmers head office took the issue of supplier rebates being used to lift profits seriously.

In the context of the broader Wesfarmers group, the amounts of money involved are not material. That is probably why Wesfarmers will not be making any statements to the ASX under the continuous disclosure rules.

One way to look at the $US10 million to $US12 million in supplier rebates is to compare these amounts with Target's cost of goods sold of more than $1 billion in the first half of the year. Also, it is possible that the rebates will be recovered in the second half and the final full-year result will not be much different to what it would have been without taking cash from suppliers in the first half.

But these excuses miss the fundamental point. Target has been a problematic subsidiary at Wesfarmers for many years.

It was well run under Launa Inman and then suffered a succession of poor profit results after she left. Machin, who replaced Dene Rogers, was meant to turn it around over four years but was replaced before his transformation was complete.

If managers at Wesfarmers feel under so much pressure to achieve results that they have to resort to squeezing suppliers to boost short-term profits then there is something wrong with the corporate culture.

Supplier rebates are a grey area when it comes to the question of financial accounting.

Bowen said the use of supplier rebates to boost profits were not in breach of accounting standards according to Bowen. But he deserves credit for taking an ethical stance that goes beyond the accounting technicalities.

The half-year accounts were reviewed by the group auditor EY.

Wesfarmers is understandably very sensitive about anything that raises doubts about its commitment to having an ethical relationship with suppliers.

In December 2014 Wesfarmers reached a settlement with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission that its supermarket subsidiary Coles had engaged in unconscionable conduct in 2011.

Coles later refunded about $12 million to its suppliers following an independent arbitration by former Victorian premier Jeff Kennett.

In the Coles case, about 200 suppliers were bullied into providing cash payments to the supermarket chain to cover "profit gaps", wastage and late delivery.

Bowen draws a distinction between what happened at Target and the unconscionable conduct case.

He said margin management was commonplace inside every retailer but Wesfarmers had to run its businesses in a way that was sustainable in the long term.

"We should not be managing for short-term profit results," he said.

Virgin in play

Air New Zealand's decision to sell its 25.9 per cent stake in Virgin Australia Holdings could be the catalyst for a takeover by one of its two other large shareholders, Etihad or Singapore Airlines.

Etihad would be the logical airline to put into a takeover scenario because of its close ties with Virgin through an international code sharing agreement and its history of taking over smaller domestic airlines.

It so happens Etihad's chief executive James Hogan is in Sydney. He is due to appear at a function in Sydney on Wednesday night, which will include Virgin's new chairman Elizabeth Bryan.

Etihad owns 25.1 per cent of Virgin and is allowed to lift its shareholding by 3 per cent every six months under the creep rules of the Corporations Act.

However, if it wished to purchase the entire Air New Zealand stake it would have to make a takeover offer or gain the approval at a Virgin shareholders' meeting.

There has been considerable tension between Air New Zealand and Virgin for some time despite the Kiwi airline's support of previous capital raisings and debt raisings by Virgin.

Its support was evident as recent as last week when Air New Zealand agreed to participate in a debt raising by Virgin as part of a long-term plan to raise more equity.

Air New Zealand chief executive Chris Luxon made it clear long ago that he believed Virgin had to have higher profitability. However, Virgin CEO John Borghetti is pursing a long-term strategy to rebuild the Virgin brand to better compete with Qantas.

Luxon's problem is that the Air New Zealand balance sheet is already too heavily exposed to a minority investment in Australia and he cannot justify making that investment any larger.

He has about $1.9 billion in equity capital, which means the $336 million stake in Virgin represents about 17 per cent of his balance sheet.

A takeover of Virgin by Etihad would enhance competition in Australia and put pressure on Qantas. Middle Eastern airlines such as Etihad tend to have easy access to capital from generous owners.

But the decline in the oil price would have put restrictions on the ability of Etihad's owners to be so free with their equity investments in the aviation industry.

HEADLINE: Findex boss Paule says all good
INTRO: An exodus of disgruntled former Crowe Horwarth and Prescott Securities partners under new owners Findex must be the topic the group's founder and boss Spiro Paule tries to avoid while he is out on the road pressing the flesh.
TEXT:
An exodus of disgruntled former Crowe Horwarth and Prescott Securities partners under new owners Findex must be the topic the group's founder and boss Spiro Paule tries to avoid while he is out on the road pressing the flesh.

Following the Easter break, Paule was back in his Sydney office on Wednesday having spent the previous two weeks on a national tour meeting with partners. It was his second internal roadshow since the January 2015 takeover.

While seven former Crowe Horwarth accountant partners have left the business since it was acquired by Findex, five have been promoted to partner, keeping partner numbers stable. Key personnel have left from Sydney, Gold Coast, and Toowoomba.

A major sticking point has been the implementation of a more centralised approach to client portfolio management, which Findex boasts has secured returns over the volatile past quarter in markets.

How smoothly the Crowe integration is progressing is likely to have a big bearing on how keen Findex's 40 per cent private equity owner KKR is to put its hand in its pocket to help shopaholic CEO Paule fund future acquisitions.

KKR-Findex has maintained a "no comment" stance on whether it is taking a look at SAS Trustee Corp's StatePlus. However Paule was happy to label the touted $1 billion plus price-tag as too high.

HEADLINE: McAleese lenders front up for short back and sides
INTRO: United States-based Anchorage Capital Group is closing in on a deal which would see McAleese's lenders take a significant haircut and equity investors wiped out completely.
TEXT:
United States-based Anchorage Capital Group is closing in on a deal which would see McAleese's lenders take a significant haircut and equity investors wiped out completely.

Street Talk understands Anchorage's plan has found favour among McAleese's syndicated lenders and a deal could be done by the end of the week. While lenders are set for meaningful losses to the face value of their $205.5 million syndicated debt, sources said the deal would be welcome relief after months of uncertainty and negotiations.

The lenders have been seeking a solution since late last year - and have been in control since McAleese announced it had blown its covenants for the December half-year balance date.

Sources stressed Anchorage's deal had yet to receive final approval - and there was still some chance the lenders could agree to terms with one of the other distressed debt firms on the scene. Sankaty Advisors is said to have re-emerged as an interested party, while Hong Kong debt trader SC Lowy has also been around the situation.

Street Talk first revealed Anchorage's interest in January. The firm is best known in Australia for taking control of timber company Gunns by buying into its debt, and playing a role in Nine Entertainment's recapitalisation.

It's understood Anchorage - and its rivals for that matter - face two options at McAleese. They can either use the company's bulk haulage and oil and gas transport business to pursue industry consolidation, or go down the liquidation route.

Either way, McAleese's existing equity investors are not likely to feature in the plans. McAleese shares have not traded since late February. Moelis & Co is advising the company.
